The turbine had a chord length (c) of 4.06 cm, a span (h) of 23.4 cm, and a preset pitch angle (α_p) of -6 degrees.
The turbine radius to the quarter chord (R) was 8.23 cm, resulting in a chord-to-radius ratio of 0.49.
The turbine blockage ratio (β) was 9.3% and the turbine solidity (σ) was 0.16 for the two-bladed configuration.
The free stream velocity (U_∞) was 0.885 m/s with a turbulence intensity between 2-3%.
The Reynolds number based on chord and free stream was 44,000.
The positively cambered foil performed worse than the symmetrical or negatively cambered foils at all but the lowest tip-speed ratios.
The negatively cambered blades reduced peak loading by 13% compared to the symmetrical blades.
The optimal tip-speed ratio was governed more by degradation in downstream performance at higher rotation rates than continued increases in upstream performance.
The peak power coefficient occurred at tip-speed ratios of around 2.8 and 2.0 for the one- and two-bladed turbines respectively, with minimal variation due to geometric camber.
The virtual camber was estimated to be around 6% and the virtual incidence was around 7 degrees for the 0.49 chord-to-radius ratio.
The position of maximum virtual camber shifted from mid-chord towards the leading edge before dramatically shifting to the aft half of the foil for azimuth angles greater than 180 degrees.
The numerical URANS simulations were used to assess a wider range of geometric camber beyond the experimental configurations.
The experimental results suggest that a small but positive total camber (geometric plus virtual) is optimal for this turbine design.
The benefits of enhanced downstream flow reattachment from the negatively cambered blades more than compensated for reduced peak power generation compared to symmetrical blades.
The study highlights the importance of considering both geometric and virtual camber effects in cross-flow turbine blade design and optimization.
